newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan racketeer scandal ensnares another brokerage.
newsitem.headline: Japan racketeer scandal ensnares another brokerage.

text.p: Japan's high-profile racketeer payoff scandal ensnared yet another top brokerage on Wednesday as prosecutors raided the offices of Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd for evidence of illegal deals.
Public broadcasting station NHK said prosecutors had raided Yamaichi headquarters in search of evidence of the misdeeds.

The move followed domestic media reports that Yamaichi provided some 80 million yen ($677,000) to Ryuichi Koike, the "sokaiya" racketeer at the heart of the scandal, in 1995 to reimburse him for losses incurred through illegal discretionary trading.

Yamaichi allegedly made the payments to obtain Koike's help in ensuring its annual shareholders' meeting went smoothly, the reports said. A Yamaichi spokesman could not immediately comment on the NHK report.

The Finance Ministry is expected to announce later on Wednesday stiff penalties against Nomura Securities -- now embroiled in its second scandal in six years -- as well as Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank, one of Japan's biggest banks, over the racketeer payoff scandal.
The penalties are expected to include orders to halt some business for as long as five months.

More than a dozen people, including top executives from the DKB and Nomura, have been arrested in the affair, which coincides with the start of "Big Bang" reforms aimed at introducing more competition and global standards into Japan's long-sheltered financial sector.

Domestic media also said on Wednesday that Tokyo prosecutors appeared to have launched investigations into the other two of Japan's "Big Four" brokerages, Daiwa Securities Co Ltd and Nikko Securities Co Ltd, in connection with the affair.
Payoffs to sokaiya have been illegal since 1993 but many Japanese companies have found it difficult to cut off ties with the underworld.

Sokaiya typically buy shares in companies and try to extort money from them by threatening to expose dubious business practices. Alternatively, they are sometimes employed by firms to quash questions from legitimate shareholders at annual meetings.
On Tuesday, the Finance Ministry said it had reprimanded two of its officials who conducted inspections of DKB for accepting favours from officials of the scandal-tainted firm.
The ministry said the acts had not affected the results of the inspection but it was necessary to maintain discipline so that inspections would not lose credibility.

The ministry came under fire when DKB's role in the scandal broke for failing to discover the dubious deals, although officials said it was virtually impossible to uncover what banks chose to hide. ($1=118 yen)
